https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Donald Trump holds a signed executive order about vaccines as the health and human services secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr looks on. Photograph: Jacquelyn Martin/AP View image in fullscreen Donald Trump holds a signed executive order about vaccines as the health and human services secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr looks on. Photograph: Jacquelyn Martin/AP Donald Trump Trump signs order attempting to override CDC vaccine schedule and break up MMR shots President and RFK Jr, the health secretary, repeatedly referred to autism during signing, though studies show no link between it and vaccines Melody Schreiber and Joseph Gedeon in Washington Mon 10 Aug 2026 18.28 EDT First published on Mon 10 Aug 2026 15.06 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Donald Trump has signed an executive order with plans for sweeping changes to the childhood vaccination schedule that attempts to override the authority of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). It is an attempt to undergird the changes made earlier this year to CDC vaccination recommendations, which were halted by a federal judge. The CDC is the federal agency tasked with recommending vaccines, not the White House. The order would also require that the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine be broken into three separate shots, once it becomes available in the US. And it would recommend that all shots be given at separate medical visits, a frequent point Trump has made despite the safety, ease and lower costs of giving vaccines together. On a press call, a White House official said the order draws on a Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) scientific assessment published in January 2026, which examined “comparisons of the U.S. to other peer-developed nations” and looked at “where there is consensus amongst our peers on recommendations for immunizations for children”. The official said the number of recommended childhood immunizations would drop “down to 11 diseases”, compared with 18 at the end of 2024. Only six of the 17 vaccines currently routinely recommended for all children in the US would continue to have full recommendations: measles, mumps, rubella ( MMR ), diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis (DTaP), polio, Hib, pneumococcal disease, HPV and varicella. “Together, there could be a possibility they’re quite lethal,” Trump said of the MMR vaccine at the signing of the order on Monday. Five other shots would be recommended only for those at high risk: monoclonal antibodies to protect against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) as well as vaccines against hepatitis A, hepatitis B and meningococcal ACWY, which is currently recommended for teens and high-risk infants. Dengue and meningococcal B vaccines are also on this list, but dengue was already recommended only for those at risk and meningococcal B was shared clinical decision-making. And six shots would be pushed to shared clinical decision-making: hepatitis A, hepatitis B, rotavirus, meningococcal disease, influenza and Covid-19. This is a previously obscure category that means a provider would be required to weigh the risks and benefits, despite strong evidence for the safety and efficacy of these vaccines. On the call, the White House official said vaccines moved into this category “still are a recommendation, and so we assume that that means they’ll still be covered by insurance” and remain “available to parents that want them”, adding: “The president is interested in getting parents more choice and flexibility.” The executive order would also require the MMR vaccine to be broken into three separate shots, which is not currently possible in the US as there are no separately licensed vaccines for measles, mumps and rubella and the licensing process takes years. The order also states that, “to the maximum extent feasible, all childhood immunizations should be administered at separate medical visits”. This would put a financial and logistical strain on families and medical providers by creating several additional visits. The US attorney general would also be tasked with challenging state laws that conflict with the executive order. The US has no vaccination mandates. Shots that are required for school attendance are set at the state and local level. Both Trump and Robert F Kennedy, the health secretary, made repeated mentions of autism throughout the order signing, emphasizing a scientifically unproven link between vaccines and the condition. Dozens of studies show no link between the two. “Today we’re proud to officially announce the United States of America’s gold standard childhood vaccination recommendations. That has to do with many subjects including autism in particular,” Trump said at the beginning of the order signing. “I’ve seen proof of it, where they have a vaccination where it looks like the size of a bottle of soda, poured into a little child’s body and bad things happen in too many cases,” Trump later said on breaking up each shot into an individual medical visit, before adding: “This is an explosion, it’s an epidemic,” in an apparent reference to autism. Kennedy claimed at one point: “Something happened in the mid-90s that changed our children, and it has to be an environmental exposure.” On the call, officials were pressed on why Kennedy has not yet delivered the finding on the cause of autism he had promised by the previous September, and why the US president continued to suggest a vaccine-autism link without new supporting evidence from HHS. An official declined to engage directly, asking to keep the discussion “germane to today’s executive order” rather than address the broader autism-research timeline. Asked about criticism from the American Academy of Pediatrics that the administration invoked autism repeatedly during the signing without offering any concrete support for families already raising children with autism, an official pointed instead to a toolkit the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Service released on applied behavior analysis services, framing it as guidance to help states serve autistic patients and curb fraud in relevant programs. Rebuking these claims and ties to autism, Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana senator, tweeted in response to the order that it “is so wrong”. “I’m a doctor. This executive order is wrong. The President does not have the expertise to make these changes. Vaccines are overwhelmingly safe. Vaccines are effective. Vaccines DO NOT cause autism. Breaking up vaccines will mean children have to get more shots to get the same protection, not fewer shots. It will increase hesitancy and make children less safe. Parents should listen to their child’s pediatrician about vaccines rather than listening to an inaccurate executive order. This is so wrong,” Cassidy wrote. Executive orders are meant as guidance to federal agencies; they are not laws passed by Congress, and thus they have no legal effect on the public. The White House official estimated that 28 states “have implemented their own vaccine recommendations or diverged from the federal guidance”. The order is intended to ensure the remaining states “are aware of this information as they go into ... their legislative sessions”, they said, and weigh “what vaccine requirements they want to implement as law in their state, particularly ... school attendance and entry requirements”. “This should have no direct operational effects,” says Dorit Reiss, a vaccines expert at UC Law San Francisco. Twenty-nine states and the District of Columbia have decoupled their vaccination requirements from the CDC, and insurance continues to cover the shots. However, “Trump has influence,” Reiss said, and the order may intensify “political pressure on states” to change school requirements. (Credit: Reuters) Police in Bulgaria evacuated nearly 200 passengers from a Viking cruise ship after the vessel ran aground due to "exceptionally low water levels" in the Danube River. The Bulgaria News Agency reported that the ship became stranded early Tuesday about 15 miles upstream from Vidin, where it planned to stop to take on supplies. Bulgarian border police ended up rescuing 186 passengers after another ship dispatched to the scene wasn’t able to get close enough to pick them up. "We can confirm that the Viking Ullur experienced a grounding incident on the Danube River on July 28, 2026, after coming into contact with a sandbank during a period of exceptionally low water levels," Viking said Friday in a statement to FOX Business. "The safety and wellbeing of our guests and crew is always our highest priority. There were no injuries, and the vessel remained safe throughout the incident," it added. "The ship was well-stocked with all necessary supplies, including food and water, to keep guests and crew safe and comfortable." Attempts to refloat the vessel Tuesday morning were unsuccessful, according to the Bulgaria News Agency. All of the passengers were from European countries and there were 52 crew members onboard as well, it added. (Reuters / Reuters) The current status of the crew members and location of the ship wasn’t immediately clear. Viking did not immediately respond to an inquiry on the matter. Viking said on its website that the Viking Ullur, built in 2019, is 443 feet long. Viking told FOX Business "there were no injuries" after the Ullur ship ran aground, and that "the vessel remained safe throughout the incident." https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqxv.text: Image source, Rune Hellestad/Getty Images By James Gregory Â and Â Paul Kirby ,Â Europe digital editor Published 27 August 2026 Norwegians have laid flowers in front of the palace in Oslo after the royal household said King Harald V's condition in hospital had become "extremely serious". His wife, Queen Sonja, and his son, Crown Prince Haakon, cancelled royal engagements to be at his bedside at Oslo University Hospital with other members of the family. They all stayed for several hours, and then during the evening Haakon was seen returning with Crown Princess Mette-Marit. The 89-year-old has been in hospital for 10 days receiving treatment for a rare blood condition, haemolytic anaemia. Late on Thursday afternoon the palace issued an update to say his condition was unchanged. Image source, EPA Image caption, Members of Norway's royal family, including King Harald's son, Crown Prince Haakon, have gathered at the hospital Having been on the throne since 1991, King Harald is Europe's oldest head of state. Crown Prince Haakon, 53, the successor to the Norwegian throne, has been serving as regent while his father is on leave. King Harald has been treated in recent weeks with cortisone for haemolytic anaemia, a condition that causes the number of red blood cells in the body to be reduced, and leads to fatigue and shortness of breath. There was a sombre mood in Oslo as Norwegians followed the comings and goings of the royal family. Crowds milled around in Palace Square throughout the day as Norwegian public TV scrapped its schedule to cover the story. Although no-one in the royal family spoke, the message was clear that it had become an important moment to visit the king. Among those visiting the hospital were Crown Princess Mette-Marit who arrived with Haakon, as well as her son Marius Borg HÃ¸iby, who is under house arrest during his appeal against a conviction for rape. King Harald's sister, Princess Astrid, also visited the hospital, along with Haakon and Mette-Marit's children Princess Ingrid Alexandra and Prince Sverre Magnus. Prime Minister Jonas Gahr StÃ¸re cancelled a planned trip to Germany, where he was expected to meet Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Thursday. "The whole nation is with us as we send warm thoughts to the king and the rest of the royal family," he said in a statement. Image source, Getty Images The king has had multiple health problems in recent years which have forced him to scale back his royal duties. He was fitted with a pacemaker in 2024 after falling ill on holiday in Malaysia. The Norwegian royal family has already faced a challenging year in 2026. Crown Princess Mette-Marit received a lung transplant in June after she had been diagnosed with a rare form of pulmonary fibrosis in 2018. The transplant came two days after HÃ¸iby was sentenced to four years in prison after being convicted of two counts of rape. He had denied the most serious charges and is to appeal the sentence. HÃ¸iby, 29, was four when his mother married Crown Prince Haakon and is not himself a royal figure. Also earlier in the year, documents were released revealing Mette-Marit's frequent contact with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. She later apologised to Norway's king and queen for her three-year friendship with Epstein and admitted to "poor judgement", adding in a national TV interview that she wished she had never met him. (is associated with: «Zelensky signs law on memorial to heroes despite protest from Poland») Michael Kappeler/dpa Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has signed a law establishing a national heroes' memorial, despite sharp criticism from Poland, according to an announcement by the Ukrainian parliament reported by the Ukrinform news agency. The so-called pantheon is set to honour members of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), nationalist underground fighters who were responsible for the mass murder of Poles and Jews - primarily in Volyn in what is now western Ukraine - during the German occupation in World War II, with tens of thousands of victims. "The Ukrainian pantheon will definitely be built, and only Ukrainians will decide who is a hero for us," Zelensky reaffirmed on Saturday before war veterans. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Under the law, the state memorial will be established in the capital Kiev and will honour historical figures dating back to the medieval Kyivan Rus empire. Internationally controversial figures whom modern Ukraine regards as independence fighters are expected to be reinterred there. The pantheon is also intended to serve as a burial site for Ukrainian presidents. The Polish government in Warsaw initially made no comment. However, the advancement of the plan could further damage relations with Poland, an important western ally of Ukraine in its fight against Russia. After the Ukrainian parliament passed the law in July, the office of Polish President Karol Nawrocki said that from Poland's perspective, glorifying criminals who had committed genocide in Volyn was not the path to the western world. Advertisement Advertisement A rift between the two countries had already emerged in June after Zelensky awarded a military unit the honorary title "Heroes of the UPA." Warsaw subsequently withdrew the Order of the White Eagle it had awarded to Zelensky. Several Ukrainian and Polish politicians also returned honours they had received from the neighbouring country. https://www.thedailybeast.com/insiders-r.text: Politics Insiders Reveal Alarming Reason Behind CIA Chief’s Trip to Russia PUTIN NOTICE John Ratcliffe flew into Moscow on a U.S. military transport aircraft. Ewan Palmer Reporter Updated Aug. 27 2026 8:58AM EDT / Published Aug. 27 2026 5:41AM EDT Comments The worrying reason CIA Director John Ratcliffe took a secret trip to Russia has been revealed. Speculation has run rampant after a U.S. military transport aircraft unexpectedly landed at a Moscow airport. It was later revealed that Ratcliffe was traveling aboard the Boeing C-17A Globemaster III in what was the CIA chief’s first publicly known visit to the Russian capital. Insiders have now told The Wall Street Journal that Ratcliffe’s trip on Tuesday was to warn Russia not to launch an unprovoked attack on NATO countries. There have been fears that Russian President Vladimir Putin, who has faced multiple humiliations as Ukraine continues to resist Russia’s invasion, could lash out by carrying out an attack ranging from a cyberattack to an incursion into a neighboring country in order to test NATO’s resolve in the coming years. Vladimir Putin has been facing numerous setbacks this year during Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Valeriy Sharifulin/via REUTERS Any scenario in which Putin attacks a member of the military alliance could have devastating consequences around the world. Under NATO’s Article 5, an attack against one NATO country is considered an attack against all 32 allied members. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed to reporters on Wednesday that Ratcliffe held talks with Russian intelligence officials during his visit, but said the CIA director did not meet with Putin. “All I can ⁠tell you is that there have been contacts via the security services. I can ​tell you that there have been no meetings with the Russian president. Naturally, President Putin is ​kept informed of everything without delay,” Peskov said. Donald Trump sought to downplay the significance of John Ratcliffe’s visit to Moscow. Kevin Lamarque/REUTERS U.S. officials previously told the Journal that it had long been assumed Putin would not provoke NATO while he was still fighting Ukraine—a conflict that has now dragged into its fifth year. However, this assessment changed earlier this year when Kyiv began fighting back with wave after wave of drone attacks that put Moscow on the back foot. Putin Nemesis Warns Russia Is Nearing ‘Breaking Point’ OIL BE DAMNED Isabel van Brugen This includes targeting Russia’s major oil refineries, which play a key role in funding the invasion, as well as warehouses and facilities used by Wildberries, Russia’s largest online retailer, to cripple Moscow’s economy. It is also believed that the U.S.’s dwindling stockpiles of munitions amid Trump’s war in Iran could influence whether Putin decides to attack a NATO country. The U.S. has also been a major supplier of weapons and munitions to Ukraine as it supports its bid to fight off the Russian invasion. Ratcliffe’s plane stopped in Riga, Latvia’s capital, on Sunday before continuing its journey to Moscow. @ALFREDSPODINS VIA X/Alfredspondis/X via REUTERS It remains to be seen how successful Ratcliffe’s trip to the Russian capital will prove to be. William Burns, who led the CIA under former President Joe Biden, was the last known intelligence agency head to visit Moscow, heading there in November 2021. Burns’ trip was to warn Putin not to attack Ukraine, which the Russian president did three months later. Heather Conley, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, said Putin would be hoping to fracture the NATO alliance with an aggressive move against one of its member states. “The question mark is how the United States would respond in that case,” Conley told the Journal. “It has always been a goal [of Russia’s] to challenge the credibility of NATO and to separate the United States from its allies.” Smoke billows from the burning Wildberries warehouse following a Ukrainian drone attack in July. Stringer/Stringer/Reuters Kremlin spokesperson Peskov tried to frame Ratcliffe’s visit as positive, saying talks between U.S. and Russian intelligence agencies could help repair the poor diplomatic relations between the two countries. “These ⁠contacts often continue even during the most difficult periods in bilateral relations. Our president, incidentally, has spoken about this. However, it is still too early to say to what extent this ⁠will, overall, ​help to steer our bilateral relations out of the ​profound crisis in which they currently find themselves,” he said. Putin’s Airports Plunged Into Chaos After CIA Chief’s Visit MOSCOW MAYHEM Isabel van Brugen President Donald Trump downplayed the significance of Ratcliffe’s Moscow visit during an interview on Glenn Beck’s radio show Wednesday. “He’s there on, you know, very sort of semi-routine. I hate to disappoint people,” Trump said. “John Ratcliffe is a fantastic guy. He’s the head of the CIA, and he is not in there for any of the things that you said. Now something may come out, you know, out of it. We’re working very hard to get that war ended.” The Daily Beast has contacted the White House and the CIA for comment. https://www.breitbart.com/politics/2026/.text: Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-MI) said during an appearance at the University of Chicago on Tuesday that she wants planned prosecutions of Trump administration figures to deter young people from taking jobs in the administration. The Michigan Democrat made the remarks at the University of Chicago’s Institute of Politics, during a live recording of Vox’s America, Actually! podcast with editorial director Astead Herndon. A clip of the exchange circulated on X. Slotkin said she wants to examine what she called “signature cases” and target not only the president but the officials around him: “I want to look at these signature cases and not just focus on the president, but on the people who enabled him,” Slotkin said. “I want young people coming out of school to say, should I go work for the Trump administration? Like that sounds fun. I might get an opportunity. I want them to be like, Lord, that might be buying myself a ton of problems that I don’t want, and so let me avoid participating in that. I want that deterrence message. The account that posted the video, @ThinkerChicago, claimed the senator hopes the planned prosecutions will frighten young conservatives away from politics altogether. In a September 30 speech to the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, Slotkin argued Democrats should pursue prosecutions of Trump officials if they retake Congress, comparing the effort to post-authoritarian cleanups in Europe. “In Poland, they called this plan the Iron Broom, cleaning the place up,” Slotkin said at the time. “The goal here is to have a list of signature cases that go after some of the most obvious and harmful abuses of taxpayer dollars.” In that speech, the former CIA officer named Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, and U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro as figures she argued should be held accountable, telling the audience that misusing taxpayer money “can land you a sentence of up to 20 years in prison.” The comments come months after Slotkin was herself the target of a Trump Justice Department investigation. Pirro’s office sought to indict the senator and five other Democrat lawmakers over a 90-second video urging military members to refuse illegal orders, which Trump called “seditious” and “punishable by death.” A federal grand jury declined to return an indictment in February.
